Contrast

GeometryParadoxesFractions
Game: Two gray bars sit on a strip that fades from dark to light, and the bars can look different even though they are painted the same gray.
How to play: Slide the five controls to change the strip and the bars, and drag the probe dot to read the gray under it.

Keyboard: Tab to the probe dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step). Each slider also has arrow keys.

Look for the math

The strip and the bars are made of nothing but grays. No colour in the picture changes when you move the sliders, yet the same flat gray can look darker beside a light strip and lighter beside a dark one. That is the simultaneous contrast illusion.

One gray, one or two bars

The page says: "Whether consisting of one or two bars, the middle shape is painted uniformly throughout." The applet agrees. It paints both rectangles with the same entry of a scale of 256 steps, numbered 0 (black) to 255 (white). If the lower and upper sliders are lo and hi, the bar's gray number is floor((lo + hi) / 2). At the opening settings, 20 and 235, that is gray 127 in both bars. The logic test checked the two rectangles for thousands of settings: their colour is always the same. What changes is only the gray around them.

Building the background strip

The strip is painted as one thin vertical line per column. Put the two colour sliders in increasing order, lo ≤ hi. Across a board w units wide, column x (from 1 to w - 3) gets gray

round(lo + (x - 1) × (hi - lo) / (w - 4))

So the first painted column is exactly lo and the last is exactly hi, whatever the width. Swapping the two sliders simply runs the ramp the other way. The page's claim that the illusion shows up "even for small ranges of the background gray" is true of the pixels too: the test checked all 255 ranges that are just one step wide, and each still paints both of its grays. A hard step from gray 120 to gray 121 is enough to change what the bars look like.

Shape barely enters it

Width, height and gap change where the bars sit, never what colour they are. The applet uses truncating division: barWidth = floor(w × W / 100), barHeight = floor(h × H / 100), gap = floor(barWidth × Gap / 100). The gap is taken out of the middle and the rest is split into two pieces; both get that same one gray. The logic test held the bar's colour fixed while sweeping every width and height and many gaps: it stayed gray 127 throughout, which is the sense of the page's "almost independently of the relative shape of the bar(s)". At W = H = 110 the single bar is larger than the board and covers it all, as the page says.

What the eye adds

The page also says a full-board bar can look gradient filled for a few seconds in a brightness afterimage, then fade on close inspection. That is a claim about seeing, not about pixels: this port keeps the bar's numbers flat and cannot time your eye. It is an optical illusion, not a trick in the drawing code. Use the probe dot to check a gray under the bar against the number reported beside it.

Try setting both gray sliders one step apart, then drag the probe from one end to the other and watch one bar appear to change while its stated gray stays put.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
